0.title: Obadiah: The Kingdom Shall Be the LORD's
0.overview:
The message. Obadiah is God’s answer to a question every wounded believer asks: did God see what was done to us, and will he do anything about it? When Jerusalem fell, Edom, Israel’s brother nation, stood by, gloated, looted and handed over the refugees. Obadiah announces that God saw it all: “The pride of your heart has deceived you” (v. 3), and “As you have done, it shall be done to you” (v. 15). Every power that thinks no one can touch it will fall, but God will keep a rescued people on Mount Zion. The book’s last words are the last word of history: “the kingdom shall be the LORD’s” (v. 21).

Background: the writer. The shortest book in the Old Testament, twenty-one verses, tells us nothing about its writer but his name, which means “servant of the LORD”. Jewish tradition identified him with the Obadiah who hid the LORD’s prophets in Ahab’s day (1 Kings 18:3–4), but nothing in the book supports this. He gives no king, no father and no home town, only “The vision of Obadiah” (v. 1).

Edom: a brother turned enemy. Edom lay south-east of the Dead Sea, a high land of red sandstone cliffs and narrow gorges; the later rock city of Petra lies in the same hills. Its people descended from Esau, the twin brother of Jacob. Before the twins were born the LORD told Rebekah, “Two nations are in your womb” (Genesis 25:23). The brothers were reconciled (Genesis 33:4), but their descendants never were, though God’s law said, “You shall not abhor an Edomite, for he is your brother” (Deuteronomy 23:7). Centuries of border wars followed. Amos condemned Edom “because he pursued his brother with the sword and cast off all pity” (Amos 1:11).

When? Obadiah names no king, so Christians differ over his date. Most place him soon after Nebuchadnezzar’s army destroyed Jerusalem in 586 BC, since verses 11–14 read like a fresh memory of that day, and other Scriptures accuse Edom of exactly this: “Remember, O LORD, against the Edomites the day of Jerusalem” (Psalm 137:7). Others place him about 845 BC, when Edom rebelled against Judah (2 Kings 8:20–22) and raiders plundered Jerusalem and the king’s house (2 Chronicles 21:16–17). Much of Obadiah runs parallel to Jeremiah’s oracle on Edom (Jeremiah 49:7–22), and scholars debate which came first. This commentary does not press a date, though the later setting explains verses 11–14 most naturally. Nothing in the message depends on the year.

The kind of writing. Obadiah is a prophetic oracle against a foreign nation, in Hebrew poetry, like those in Isaiah 13–23 and Jeremiah 46–51. Such oracles were spoken less to the nations named than to God’s own people: Edom probably never heard this book, but Judah did, among the ruins. It speaks of the future as already done, because God has said it, and it sees one nation’s reckoning as a preview of “the day of the LORD” on all the nations (v. 15).

How the book makes its case. First comes the verdict (verses 1–9): God summons the nations against Edom and strips away everything it trusted, one layer at a time: its fortress “in the clefts of the rock” (v. 3), its hidden treasure, its allies, its wise men and its soldiers. Then comes the charge (verses 10–14): “the violence done to your brother Jacob” (v. 10). Edom “stood aloof” while strangers looted Jerusalem, and God’s verdict on the bystander is “you were like one of them” (v. 11). Eight commands trace a terrible progression, from gloating and boasting to looting and at last catching the fugitives at the crossroads to hand them over. What began with a look ended in murder. Last comes the horizon (verses 15–21): the day of the LORD on every nation, with exact repayment as its rule. But judgment is not the last word: “But in Mount Zion there shall be those who escape, and it shall be holy” (v. 17). The scattered exiles come home to more than they lost, and “Saviors shall go up to Mount Zion to rule Mount Esau, and the kingdom shall be the LORD’s” (v. 21).

A hard word against a nation? Verse 18, with “no survivor for the house of Esau”, is hard to read. But the book is not a curse spoken in revenge. It is God’s sentence on a people who showed no mercy, and it leaves the reckoning with God, as the New Testament does: “Beloved, never avenge yourselves, but leave it to the wrath of God” (Romans 12:19). History bore it out: within a few generations Edom’s kingdom had collapsed, Arab peoples such as the Nabataeans took its hills, and its people, pushed west into southern Judah (later called Idumea), vanish from history after the first century AD. Yet the door was never shut to Edomites themselves: Amos heard God promise that the restored house of David would possess “the remnant of Edom” (Amos 9:12). This commentary’s view is that the nation which fought God’s people perished, while sinners from every nation, Israel’s old enemies included, are welcomed in Christ.

Where Christians differ. How is the promise of land in verses 19–20 fulfilled? Dispensationalists look for a literal future possession by the nation of Israel. This commentary reads it, with the New Testament, as fulfilled in part in the return from exile and fully in Christ’s kingdom, whose meek “shall inherit the earth” (Matthew 5:5).

Where it leads: to Christ. Obadiah leads to Christ by the need it exposes, by contrast and by promise. The need: if the rule of the last day is “As you have done, it shall be done to you” (v. 15), none of us could stand. The cup of judgment in verse 16 is the cup Jesus faced in Gethsemane: “My Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me; nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will” (Matthew 26:39). At the cross he received what we had done, so that we might receive what he deserved. The contrast: Edom stood aloof from its brother on the day of his ruin, but Christ came down into ours, and “he is not ashamed to call them brothers” (Hebrews 2:11). The promise: the rescued people on Mount Zion are those who trust him, for “you have come to Mount Zion and to the city of the living God” and “to Jesus, the mediator of a new covenant” (Hebrews 12:22, 24). When James quoted Amos at the council in Jerusalem, he followed the Greek Old Testament, which read “Edom” as “mankind”: “that the remnant of mankind may seek the Lord, and all the Gentiles who are called by my name” (Acts 15:17). Edom’s remnant had widened into the world. Later still, Herod the Great, a king of Edomite descent, tried to kill the infant Jesus (Matthew 2:16), and failed. The end Obadiah saw will be announced in heaven: “The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ” (Revelation 11:15).

For us. To anyone who has been wronged and wondered whether God noticed, Obadiah says that he saw every detail and that the reckoning may be left to him. To anyone tempted to stand aloof, or to enjoy the fall of someone they resent, it says that God counts the bystander among the attackers, and that gloating is where cruelty begins. The gospel cuts the root of it, because at the cross we learn that we are not spectators at someone else’s judgment: we deserved it, and Christ took our place. And they need not fear the powers that look unshakeable, for “God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble” (James 4:6), and the kingdom shall be the LORD’s.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — The Pride of Your Heart
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Pride deceives, and God will bring down every height that people trust instead of him. The LORD himself stirs up the nations against Edom and settles its future in one sentence (vv. 1–2). Then he exposes the lie at the root: Edom thought its cliff fortress put it beyond anyone’s reach, but no nest is set so high that God cannot bring it down (vv. 3–4). One by one he removes everything Edom trusted. Treasure that thieves would have left is searched out, and allies who ate at its table set the trap (vv. 5–7). Its famous wise men lose their understanding and its soldiers their nerve (vv. 8–9). What looked unshakeable collapses from within.
verseByVerse.theology: Pride deceives, and no height, wealth or cleverness can keep anyone safe from God.

verseByVerse.quote: The vision of Obadiah. Thus says the Lord GOD concerning Edom: We have heard a report from the LORD, and a messenger has been sent among the nations: "Rise up! Let us rise against her for battle!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Obadiah’s vision is God’s own word about Edom, and it opens with news that the LORD is already stirring up the nations against her.

The vision of Obadiah. We know nothing about Obadiah except his name: no king, no date, no family (see the introduction). What we have is a “vision” from God “concerning Edom”, and “Thus says the Lord GOD” puts the authority where it belongs.

A messenger has been sent among the nations. The prophet has overheard heaven’s news: a messenger is stirring up the nations for war against Edom. Nations imagine they choose their own wars; God is the one who moves them. For a people among the ruins this was the first comfort: before they had finished grieving, God had already acted.

The date. Most date the book soon after the Babylonians destroyed Jerusalem in 586 BC, a day Psalm 137:7 remembers against Edom; others about 845 BC, when Edom rebelled against Judah (2 Kings 8:20–22) and raiders plundered Jerusalem (2 Chronicles 21:16–17) (see the introduction). Nothing in the message depends on settling it. Either way, the first hearers had watched a brother nation turn on them in their worst hour, and the vision assured them that God had seen it all and that the last word was his (v. 21).

Obadiah and Jeremiah. Much of Obadiah is very like Jeremiah’s oracle on Edom (Jeremiah 49:7–22). Which came first is debated (see the introduction); the message is the same either way.
verseByVerse.note: The name Obadiah means "servant of the LORD"; about a dozen different men in the Old Testament bear it.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, I will make you small among the nations; you shall be utterly despised. The pride of your heart has deceived you, you who live in the clefts of the rock, in your lofty dwelling, who say in your heart, "Who will bring me down to the ground?" Though you soar aloft like the eagle, though your nest is set among the stars, from there I will bring you down, declares the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Edom thinks its heights make it untouchable, but its pride has lied to it, and God will bring it down from wherever it nests.

I will make you small among the nations. Edom’s future is settled in one sentence: the nation that looked down on its brother will be small and “utterly despised”.

The pride of your heart has deceived you. Pride is a liar. It tells us we are safe, self-sufficient and beyond correction, and by the time we discover otherwise it is too late.

You who live in the clefts of the rock. Edom’s pride rested on where it lived: the high red sandstone country south-east of the Dead Sea, cliffs reached through narrow gorges, where the later rock city of Petra was carved. It is one thing to feel secure; it is another to say in your heart, “Who will bring me down to the ground?”, as if nobody, not even God, could touch you.

Though you soar aloft like the eagle. However high Edom sets its nest, God reaches higher. The same charge was laid against the king of Babylon, who said, “I will ascend to heaven; above the stars of God I will set my throne on high” (Isaiah 14:13).

A brother nation. The Edomites descended from Esau, the twin brother of Jacob (Genesis 36:1; see the introduction). Esau lost the blessing and “hated Jacob” (Genesis 27:41), and though the brothers themselves were reconciled (Genesis 33:4), their descendants kept the quarrel alive for a thousand years. Edom refused Israel passage on the way to the promised land (Numbers 20:18), though God’s law said, “You shall not abhor an Edomite, for he is your brother” (Deuteronomy 23:7).

The one who came down. Edom climbed towards the stars and was brought down. The Son of God, who truly dwelt on high, came down of his own will and “humbled himself by becoming obedient to the point of death”, and God “highly exalted him” (Philippians 2:8–9). In God’s kingdom the way up is the way down.

Our own fortresses. Our fortresses are usually not cliffs but savings, qualifications, reputation, health or family. None of them is wrong in itself, and all of them can quietly make us feel that no one could ever bring us down. “God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble” (James 4:6), and Jesus said, “everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, but the one who humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke 18:14). It is far better to come down willingly now, into the arms of the God who gives grace to the humble, than to be brought down at the last.

Was Edom doomed from birth? Readers who know Malachi’s words, “I have loved Jacob but Esau I have hated” (Malachi 1:2–3), which Paul uses of God’s free choice in grace (Romans 9:13), may wonder. Obadiah does not argue that way. He names what Edom did, its pride and its cruelty to a brother, and judges it for that. God’s free choice and real human guilt stand side by side in Scripture, and neither cancels the other.

Uncertain wording. The ESV notes that verse 2 may be read “I have made you small”, the prophet speaking of what God has decided as already done. It also notes that “the rock” (Hebrew sela) may be a place name, Sela, a rock stronghold of Edom. Neither changes the meaning.
verseByVerse.note: Sela is probably the rock stronghold that King Amaziah of Judah captured and renamed Joktheel (2 Kgs 14:7).

verseByVerse.quote: If thieves came to you, if plunderers came by night— how you have been destroyed!— would they not steal only enough for themselves? If grape gatherers came to you, would they not leave gleanings? How Esau has been pillaged, his treasures sought out! All your allies have driven you to your border; those at peace with you have deceived you; they have prevailed against you; those who eat your bread have set a trap beneath you— you have no understanding.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When God judges Edom, nothing will be left: its hidden treasure will be searched out, and the friends it trusted will betray it.

If thieves came to you. Obadiah uses two pictures from ordinary life. Thieves take what they can carry and leave the rest; grape pickers always miss a few bunches, and the poor came behind to gather them. When God deals with Edom, nothing will be left. Its hidden “treasures”, stored in caves and cliff strongholds, will be “sought out”. The prophet breaks into his own sentence with a cry, “how you have been destroyed!”, speaking as if it had already happened, because God has said it.

Those at peace with you have deceived you. Edom sat on important trade routes and knew how to make friends with the strong. Now those friends, the ones at the dinner table, set the trap: Edom, who betrayed a brother, is betrayed by friends. In time Edom was indeed driven from its ancient territory, probably by Arab peoples such as the Nabataeans in the centuries after the exile, and had to settle further west in southern Judah, which came to be called Idumea.

You have no understanding. Edom was famous for its clever men, yet it had “no understanding” of this. Cleverness has no answer when God acts.

Uncertain wording. The last line of verse 7 is compressed in Hebrew. The words “those who eat” are supplied, the ESV notes that the verb may be read “he has set a trap”, and the word translated “trap” is rare (the KJV has “wound”). The sense is clear: those Edom trusted most turned against it.

verseByVerse.quote: Will I not on that day, declares the LORD, destroy the wise men out of Edom, and understanding out of Mount Esau? And your mighty men shall be dismayed, O Teman, so that every man from Mount Esau will be cut off by slaughter.
verseByVerse.commentary:
On the day God acts, Edom’s famous wisdom and its warriors’ courage will fail together, and nothing will stand between Edom and its fall.

Destroy the wise men out of Edom. Edom had a reputation for wisdom. Jeremiah asks, “Is wisdom no more in Teman?” (Jeremiah 49:7), and Job’s friend Eliphaz was a Temanite, from Edomite territory (Job 2:11). Wisdom is God’s gift, and he can withdraw it: a nation can lose the ability to think clearly about its own danger.

Your mighty men shall be dismayed. The soldiers’ courage will be gone before the battle. One layer at a time God takes away the cliffs (vv. 3–4), the hidden treasure (vv. 5–6), the allies (v. 7), the wise men (v. 8), and now the soldiers. It is a sober picture of what happens when God finally deals with human pride: not a fair fight, but a quiet collapse.

The wisdom that does not fail. Paul quotes Isaiah’s similar warning, “I will destroy the wisdom of the wise” (1 Corinthians 1:19), and points to the wisdom God has not withdrawn: “Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Corinthians 1:24). The message of the cross, foolish as it looks, is the one wisdom that saves.
verseByVerse.note: Teman, named after a grandson of Esau (Gen 36:11), often stands for Edom as a whole.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–14 — The Day of Your Brother
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s charge against Edom is that it turned on its own brother in his worst hour, and he counts the watcher among the attackers. The violence was done to “your brother Jacob”, so shame will cover Edom forever (v. 10). On the day Jerusalem fell, Edom did not need to swing a sword to be guilty: it stood aloof while strangers looted and gambled for the city, and God’s verdict is “you were like one of them” (v. 11). Then eight commands, each beginning “do not”, retrace what Edom did, step by step: gloating, rejoicing and boasting, entering the gate and looting, and at last catching the fugitives at the crossroads and handing them over (vv. 12–14). What began with a look ended in murder.
verseByVerse.theology: Standing by while others suffer, and gloating over a brother's ruin, are sins God takes personally.

verseByVerse.quote: Because of the violence done to your brother Jacob, shame shall cover you, and you shall be cut off forever. On the day that you stood aloof, on the day that strangers carried off his wealth and foreigners entered his gates and cast lots for Jerusalem, you were like one of them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Edom’s crime was violence against its own brother, and God counts the one who stood by and watched as one of the attackers.

Your brother Jacob. The key word in the charge is “brother”. God had protected Edom’s land when Israel marched to Canaan (Deuteronomy 2:4–5) and forbidden Israel to abhor them (Deuteronomy 23:7). Edom’s violence was against family, so the nation that enjoyed its brother’s disgrace will be covered with its own shame. God notices what families and churches do to their own: the closer the tie, the deeper the wound, and the more seriously he takes it.

On the day that you stood aloof. Here is the scene. Jerusalem has fallen. Foreign soldiers pour through the broken gates, carry off everything of value and cast lots for the city as if it were a prize. And where was Edom? “You stood aloof.” In verse 11 they do not even swing a sword; they simply stand and watch their brother being destroyed.

You were like one of them. In God’s eyes the bystander had joined the attackers. Standing aside is a choice. It was the sin of the priest and the Levite who passed by on the other side and left the wounded man (Luke 10:31–32), and the sin John describes when he asks how God’s love can abide in anyone who “sees his brother in need, yet closes his heart against him” (1 John 3:17). “So whoever knows the right thing to do and fails to do it, for him it is sin” (James 4:17).

The brother who did not stand aloof. Edom kept its distance from its brother on the day of his ruin. Christ took our flesh and blood and “is not ashamed to call them brothers” (Hebrews 2:11); he did not watch our ruin from a safe height, but entered it and bore it.

What it does not mean. Not guilt for every suffering we cannot reach. Edom was near, able to help, and chose to watch; the sin is closing the heart to a need in front of us and in our power to meet (Proverbs 3:27).

verseByVerse.quote: But do not gloat over the day of your brother in the day of his misfortune; do not rejoice over the people of Judah in the day of their ruin; do not boast in the day of distress. Do not enter the gate of my people in the day of their calamity; do not gloat over his disaster in the day of his calamity; do not loot his wealth in the day of his calamity. Do not stand at the crossroads to cut off his fugitives; do not hand over his survivors in the day of distress.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Each “do not” names something Edom actually did, and together they show how sin grows: from a pleased look at a brother’s ruin to handing his survivors over to the enemy.

The day of your brother. The word “day” beats through these commands like a drum. God is not giving Edom advice for next time; each command describes a crime Edom had already committed.

How sin grows. Watch the progression, because it is the way sin always grows. It begins in the eyes: “do not gloat”. Then it reaches the heart: “do not rejoice”. Then it comes out of the mouth: “do not boast” (the ESV notes the Hebrew is vivid, “do not enlarge your mouth”). Then the feet move: “Do not enter the gate of my people”. Then the hands take: “do not loot his wealth”. Finally the worst of all: standing “at the crossroads” to catch the refugees running for their lives, and handing the survivors over to the enemy. What began as a look ended in murder.

The gate of my people. In the middle of this God calls Judah “my people”. Even in the hour when he was judging them, they were still his, and he was watching how others treated them.

The pleasure of watching someone fall. Few of us will ever plunder a city. But the quiet pleasure at the downfall of someone we resent (the colleague who failed, the church that split, the relative whose marriage collapsed) is the very sin God names first. German calls it Schadenfreude, and our culture has built an industry on it: a stranger’s worst moment can be watched, shared and mocked by millions before nightfall. It feels good because another’s fall quietly tells me I am better than him: self-justification on the cheap: I have not done much, but at least I am not her. That is why religious people are as prone to it as anyone; it is the moralist’s favourite pleasure, and the cynic’s too. Scripture says plainly, “Do not rejoice when your enemy falls, and let not your heart be glad when he stumbles” (Proverbs 24:17).

The gospel cuts the root. The gloating heart is only a beginning, but a real one. The answer is not despair but the gospel, which tells us we have no standing of our own to protect. We are not spectators at someone else’s judgment; we were the ones who deserved it, and Christ came down from the heights and took our place in the ruins. So when we find that pleasure in ourselves, we confess it to the Christ who prayed for those who mocked him (Luke 23:34), and whose Spirit teaches us to “weep with those who weep” (Romans 12:15). People who know they have been rescued cannot easily enjoy someone else’s fall. They are too busy being grateful that they were caught.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew form of these commands normally forbids something not yet done, yet verse 11 shows that Edom had already done these things. So some translations make them rebukes for the past (you should not have gloated), while the ESV keeps them as commands, the prophet reliving the scene. Either way God names what Edom did and declares it wrong.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–21 — The Kingdom Shall Be the LORD's
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: History will end not with the proud on top but with God’s rescued people safe and his kingdom established. The day of the LORD comes on every nation, and its rule is exact justice: what Edom did will return on its own head, and the cup drunk on God’s holy mountain will pass to all the nations as the cup of judgment (vv. 15–16). But Mount Zion will have survivors, made holy and given back their possessions, while the house of Esau burns like stubble (vv. 17–18). The scattered exiles will possess more than they lost, in every direction of the compass (vv. 19–20), and saviours will go up to Mount Zion to rule the height that thought itself untouchable, for “the kingdom shall be the LORD’s” (v. 21).
verseByVerse.theology: History ends not with Edom or any empire, but with salvation on Mount Zion and the kingdom of God.

verseByVerse.quote: For the day of the LORD is near upon all the nations. As you have done, it shall be done to you; your deeds shall return on your own head. For as you have drunk on my holy mountain, so all the nations shall drink continually; they shall drink and swallow, and shall be as though they had never been.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The day of the LORD is coming on every nation, and on that day what each has done will come back on its own head. The cup drunk in triumph on God’s hill will become the cup of his judgment for all the nations.

Near upon all the nations. The message suddenly widens from one small nation to “all the nations”. What God does to Edom he will do to every proud and cruel power, because he is the God of the whole earth.

As you have done, it shall be done to you. The rule of that day is simple. Edom cut off fugitives (v. 14), and Edom will be cut off (vv. 9–10). Edom looted (v. 13), and Edom will be pillaged (v. 6). Jesus stated the same principle: “with the measure you use it will be measured to you” (Matthew 7:2), and Paul warned, “whatever one sows, that will he also reap” (Galatians 6:7).

As you have drunk on my holy mountain. The word “drunk” may look back to revelling on God’s temple hill while Jerusalem burned, and it points to the cup of God’s wrath that the prophets often describe: “in the hand of the LORD there is a cup with foaming wine” (Psalm 75:8), which God made the nations drink (Jeremiah 25:15–17). Most likely both are in view: the cup of triumph becomes the cup of judgment. The end is total: they will be “as though they had never been”.

The cup Christ drank. None of us would survive a judgment that gave us back exactly what we have given others. The only escape from that cup is that someone else drank it. In Gethsemane Jesus prayed, “My Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me; nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will” (Matthew 26:39), and then said, “shall I not drink the cup that the Father has given me?” (John 18:11). At the cross he received what we had done, so that we might receive what he deserved. He drank it to the dregs for his people.

What it does not mean. “As you have done, it shall be done to you” is the rule of God’s judgment, not a licence for us to repay. The wronged are told to leave it with him: “Beloved, never avenge yourselves, but leave it to the wrath of God” (Romans 12:19).

Uncertain wording. Edom has been addressed as “you” in the singular, but the “you” of verse 16 is plural. Some take it as Edom and its allies carousing on the captured hill; others think the words now turn to Judah, who drank the cup of judgment on God’s mountain, which all the nations must now drink. On either reading the cup passes to every nation that has set itself against God.

verseByVerse.quote: But in Mount Zion there shall be those who escape, and it shall be holy, and the house of Jacob shall possess their own possessions. The house of Jacob shall be a fire, and the house of Joseph a flame, and the house of Esau stubble; they shall burn them and consume them, and there shall be no survivor for the house of Esau, for the LORD has spoken.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Judgment is not the last word: God will keep a rescued, holy people on Mount Zion and give back what was taken, while proud Edom burns like stubble.

In Mount Zion there shall be those who escape. Verse 17 begins with “But”, one of the great words of the Bible. On the hill where Edom’s allies had celebrated, God will keep a rescued people. Joel says the same: “in Mount Zion and in Jerusalem there shall be those who escape” (Joel 2:32), and adds the promise that “everyone who calls on the name of the LORD shall be saved”.

It shall be holy. Zion will be cleansed of everything that defiled it, and “the house of Jacob shall possess their own possessions”: God’s people will get back what was taken from them.

The house of Esau stubble. Edom had seemed as permanent as its cliffs; before God’s people it will prove as flimsy as dry stubble before a flame. “The house of Jacob” and “the house of Joseph” are the southern and northern tribes together, reunited in God’s purpose.

The Zion we have come to. Believers have already come to that holy mountain: “you have come to Mount Zion and to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem”, and “to Jesus, the mediator of a new covenant” (Hebrews 12:22, 24). Those who escape are those who have fled to him.

Facing hard words. These are hard words, and honesty requires us to feel their weight. They are God’s sentence on a nation that had shown no mercy, and Edom did eventually disappear as a people. Yet even here the door is not shut against individual Edomites: the restored kingdom of David would include “the remnant of Edom” (Amos 9:12; Acts 15:16–17). The nation that fought God’s people perished; sinners from every nation, Israel’s old enemies included, are welcomed in Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: Those of the Negeb shall possess Mount Esau, and those of the Shephelah shall possess the land of the Philistines; they shall possess the land of Ephraim and the land of Samaria, and Benjamin shall possess Gilead. The exiles of this host of the people of Israel shall possess the land of the Canaanites as far as Zarephath, and the exiles of Jerusalem who are in Sepharad shall possess the cities of the Negeb. Saviors shall go up to Mount Zion to rule Mount Esau, and the kingdom shall be the LORD's.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s scattered people will be given back more than they lost, and saviours from Zion will rule the proud height of Edom, because in the end the kingdom belongs to the LORD.

Those of the Negeb shall possess Mount Esau. The verses sweep around the compass. The Negeb is the dry south, the Shephelah the low hills west towards Philistia, Ephraim and Samaria the central highlands, and Gilead the land east of the Jordan. Zarephath lay up the coast in Phoenicia, where Elijah once stayed with a widow (1 Kings 17:9). The point of the list is not geography but reversal: the people who lost everything will be given more than they lost, and the scattered exiles will come home.

Saviors shall go up to Mount Zion. “Saviors” is the word used for the deliverers God raised up in the days of the judges (Judges 3:9; Nehemiah 9:27): men who rescued his people when they cried to him. From Zion they rule “Mount Esau”, the proud height that thought itself untouchable.

The kingdom shall be the LORD’s. The book ends in one magnificent line, which is the point of the whole book. The kingdom belongs not to Edom, Babylon or any power that seems to own the future, but to God. Zechariah says it too: “the LORD will be king over all the earth” (Zechariah 14:9).

How it comes about. The New Testament shows how. There is one Saviour who went up to Mount Zion, and he is the Lord himself. Jesus Christ was crucified outside Jerusalem, rose and ascended to reign, and he shares his reign with his people (Revelation 3:21): the saviours of verse 21 are fulfilled in him and in those who belong to him. At the end the announcement rings out, “The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ, and he shall reign forever and ever” (Revelation 11:15). Centuries after Obadiah, Herod the Great, a king of Edomite descent, tried to kill the infant Jesus (Matthew 2:16). Esau’s line made one last attempt on the child of Jacob’s line, and failed. Within about a century the Idumeans, as Edom’s descendants were then called, had vanished from history; the King they tried to kill reigns forever. His kingdom has begun and will be complete when he returns.

Three things to keep. So this little book leaves the believer, who has been shown mercy, with three things. Do not be proud, because God brings the high down. Do not gloat over anyone’s fall, because God is watching how we treat our brothers. And do not fear the Edoms of this world, however secure they look: the kingdom shall be the LORD’s.

Where Christians differ: how is the possession of these lands fulfilled? Dispensationalists look for a literal future possession by the nation of Israel, reading the land promises as still awaiting fulfilment for the nation. This commentary’s view: it was fulfilled in part in the return after the exile and fully in Christ’s kingdom, where his people inherit the earth (Matthew 5:5), for the New Testament widens the land promises in Christ to the whole earth (Romans 4:13); faithful Christians differ here.

Uncertain wording. The first half of verse 20 is compressed in Hebrew, and translations differ over who “this host” of exiles is and where they are. “Sepharad” cannot be identified with certainty. It has often been connected with Sardis in Asia Minor, and Jewish readers in the Middle Ages took it to mean Spain, which is why Jews of Spanish descent are still called Sephardic. The main sense is clear: exiles scattered far from home will return and possess the land.

1.title: The Kingdom Shall Be the LORD's
1.overview:
Where we are. Obadiah has only one chapter, so this chapter is the whole book, the shortest in the Old Testament. Jerusalem has fallen, and Edom, the nation descended from Jacob’s brother Esau, has stood by, gloated and joined in.

The message. God saw everything that was done to his people, and he will answer it. Pride that thinks itself beyond reach will be brought down, and cruelty done to a brother will come back on the one who did it. But judgment is not the last word: God will keep a rescued, holy people on Mount Zion, and “the kingdom shall be the LORD’s” (v. 21).

Why it was said. The first hearers were survivors of Judah among the ruins, who had watched their own kin loot the city and hand over the refugees (see the introduction). Had God noticed, and would the proud and the cruel have the last word?

How the chapter makes its case. First the verdict: God stirs up the nations against Edom, exposes the pride that made it feel safe in its cliffs, and strips away everything it trusted (vv. 1–9). Then the charge: violence against “your brother Jacob”, beginning with standing aloof on the day Jerusalem fell and growing from a gloating look to handing over the fugitives (vv. 10–14). Last the horizon: the day of the LORD on every nation, with exact repayment as its rule (vv. 15–16), and beyond it a holy Zion with survivors (vv. 17–18), exiles given back more than they lost, and saviours ruling from Mount Zion in the LORD’s kingdom (vv. 19–21).

Where it leads. To Christ in three honest ways. By the need it exposes: if the rule of the last day is “As you have done, it shall be done to you” (v. 15), none of us could stand, and the cup of judgment in verse 16 is the cup Jesus drank at the cross. By contrast: Edom stood aloof on its brother’s day of ruin, but the Son of God came down into ours and “is not ashamed to call them brothers” (Hebrews 2:11). And by promise: the rescued people on Mount Zion are those who have come “to Jesus, the mediator of a new covenant” (Hebrews 12:24), and the saviours of verse 21 are fulfilled in the one Saviour whose kingdom has no end.

For us. If you have been wronged, God saw every detail, and the reckoning can be left with him. If you are tempted to stand aloof, or to enjoy the fall of someone you resent, God counts the bystander among the attackers, and the gospel cuts the root of that pleasure: Christ took our place in the ruins. And no power that looks unshakeable need be feared: the kingdom is the LORD’s.
1.theology:
God rules the nations and moves them as he wills, even when they think they are choosing their own wars (v. 1).

Pride deceives; no fortress, wealth or cleverness can protect anyone from God, who opposes the proud (vv. 3-4, 8-9; Isa 14:13-14; Jas 4:6; Luke 18:14).

God takes wrongs done within the family of his people personally, and counts the bystander among the attackers (vv. 10-11; Luke 10:31-32; 1 John 3:17; Jas 4:17).

Gloating over another's downfall is sin, and it is where cruelty begins (vv. 12-14; Prov 24:17-18).

God repays what people have done, and Christ drank the cup of that judgment in his people's place (vv. 15-16; Matt 7:2; Gal 6:7; Ps 75:8; Matt 26:39; John 18:11).

God preserves a people who escape, and makes Zion holy; believers have come to the heavenly Zion in Christ (v. 17; Joel 2:32; Heb 12:22-24).

Judgment on hostile nations and mercy to individuals from them belong together: a remnant of Edom is promised to the kingdom of David's Son (v. 18; Amos 9:12; Acts 15:16-17).

History ends with salvation on Mount Zion and with God's kingdom, established by Jesus Christ, the true Savior and King (v. 21; Judg 3:9; Zech 14:9; Rev 11:15).
1.examples:
Edom nested in its cliffs and asked who could ever bring it down. God answered by taking away, one by one, everything it trusted, until even the friends at its table set a trap for it. Our own fortresses are more often savings, reputation or health than rock, and they can be held humbly or proudly.

Edom's sin began with a brother standing at a distance, watching a city burn; the look became a cheer, the cheer a robbery, and the robbery ended with refugees caught at the crossroads. The quiet pleasure we take in someone's fall is the same sin at its beginning, and it can be confessed to the Christ who prayed for those who mocked him.

The cup Edom passed round in triumph became the cup of judgment, and Christ drank that cup for his people. So the book ends not with stubble where a fortress stood but with saviors on Zion and a kingdom that belongs to God alone.

keyVerse.quote: Saviors shall go up to Mount Zion to rule Mount Esau, and the kingdom shall be the LORD’s.
keyVerse.note: The book’s last line is its whole point. Edom thought the future belonged to the strong and the secure; God answers that it belongs to him, and that rescue, not ruin, has the last word on Mount Zion. The saviours Obadiah foresaw find their fulfilment in the one Saviour, Jesus Christ, who reigns now and whose kingdom every nation will one day acknowledge.

1.reflection:
Edom felt safe “in the clefts of the rock” and asked, “Who will bring me down to the ground?” (v. 3). What are the heights people trust in today, and how can we tell when a good gift such as savings, health or reputation has become a fortress against God?

God’s verdict on the bystander is “you were like one of them” (v. 11). Where are we most tempted to stand aloof from a brother or sister in trouble, in church, family or online, and what would it look like to come near instead?

Verses 12–14 trace sin from a look to the betrayal of refugees. Why is quiet pleasure at someone else’s fall so attractive, and how does the cross take away our need for it?

The book ends, “the kingdom shall be the LORD’s” (v. 21). How can this hope help someone who has been badly wronged to leave justice with God, rather than either taking revenge or giving up?
